name: spigot
why: Streaming exact real calculator by Simon Tatham that prints digits of pi, e and others forever without ever rounding, a real door into exact arithmetic.

brief.what_it_is: spigot is a command-line streaming exact real calculator by Simon Tatham. You give it a mathematical expression, and it prints digits of the result one at a time, including constants such as pi and e, and keeps going until you stop it. It can also read numbers from a file or a pipe and start producing output once it has read enough input to know how the output begins.
brief.why_it_exists: Ordinary calculators need to know in advance how many digits you want, and rounding errors pile up across successive operations so the last digits can be wrong. spigot's author frames it as a tool that outputs no digit until it is sure that digit is right, and that is useful when you need very many digits or want a cross-check on other calculating systems.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage names the core algorithm as Jeremy Gibbons's unbounded spigot algorithm for the digits of pi, which spigot extends to more output modes and many more input numbers. The page does not explain the internals beyond that. Its streaming behaviour means output starts as soon as enough input has been read to determine the start of the result.

commands_seen.context: Checks out the development sources from the author's git repository, for anyone who wants the latest state of development rather than the release tarball.

brief.install_notes: The homepage offers a Unix source archive, spigot-20261009.b2c2295.tar.gz, which implies building from source, though the build steps are not on the homepage and I did not open the manual or the README in the repository. A pre-compiled spigot.exe is provided for Windows. The brew formula installs an executable named spigot. No accounts, runtimes or configuration are mentioned on the homepage.
brief.standout: Most calculators give you a fixed-precision answer with silent rounding error. spigot instead promises that every digit it prints is correct and that it will keep producing digits without limit, which makes exact arithmetic on constants like pi a usable command-line activity.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage was last modified on Fri Oct 9 2026 and the source archive is dated 20261009, which suggests recent activity. The homepage gives no release history, so this rests on those two dates.
brief.caveats: The page says spigot is very slow compared with ordinary computer arithmetic. The Unix build is distributed as a source tarball, and the homepage gives no build instructions. Bug reports go to anakin@pobox.com, and the page asks readers to read an article before reporting a bug. The first fetch of the homepage failed with a URLError and the second attempt succeeded, so the homepage was reachable only intermittently during this read.
quotes: spigot, by contrast, does not output any digit of the answer until it's sure that the digit is right, and it will keep generating digits until you tell it to stop.
The downside is that spigot is very slow compared to the usual kind of computer arithmetic.
spigot is named after its core algorithm, which is Jeremy Gibbons's unbounded spigot algorithm for the digits of π
